ety.text: From Middle English juge, jugge, from Old French juge, from Latin iūdex. Displaced native Middle English deme (from Old English dēma (“judge”)) and demere (from Old English dēmere (“judge”)), see also deemer, deemster.

chain.g: to examine judicially, judge, pass judgement, decide; condemn

ety.text: From Middle English jugen, borrowed from Anglo-Norman juger, from Old French jugier, from Latin iūdicāre. Doublet of judicate. Partly displaced native deem.

senses.d: A public official whose duty it is to administer the law, especially by presiding over trials and rendering judgments; a justice.
A person who decides the fate of someone or something that has been called into question.
A person officiating at a sports event, a contest, or similar; referee.
ex: At a boxing match, the decision of the judges is final.

senses.d: A person who evaluates something or forms an opinion.
ex: She is a good judge of wine.
They say he is a poor judge of character considering all the unreliable friends he has made.

senses.d: A shophet, a temporary leader appointed in times of crisis in ancient Israel.
To sit in judgment on; to pass sentence on (a person or matter).
ex: A higher power will judge you after you are dead.

senses.d: To sit in judgment, to act as judge.
ex: Justices in this country judge without appeal.

senses.d: To judicially rule or determine.
To sentence to punishment, to judicially condemn.
ex: He was judged to die for his crimes.

senses.d: To award judicially; to adjudge.
To form an opinion on; to appraise.
ex: I judge a man’s character by the cut of his suit.
Let us be judged for what we attempted rather than what we achieved.

senses.d: To constitute a fitting appraisal or criterion of; to provide a basis for forming an opinion on.
ex:
Noble and milde this Perſean ſeemes to be,
If outward habit Iudge the inward man.

senses.d: To arbitrate; to pass opinion on something, especially to settle a dispute etc.
ex: We cannot both be right: you must judge between us.

senses.d: To have as an opinion; to consider, suppose.
ex: I judge it safe to leave the house once again.
I've been judged to have the best qualifications.

senses.d: To form an opinion; to infer.
ex: I judge from the sky that it might rain later.
However I have the mirror positioned, I can't judge where the back of the car is.

to sit in judgment on, act as judge

ety.text: From Middle English juggement, borrowed from Old French jugement, from Late Latin iūdicāmentum, from Latin iūdicō. Partially displaced doom. By surface analysis, judge + -ment.

senses.d: The act of judging.
ex: The key to the situation was judgment of the role the railways could play in modern times.

senses.d: The power or faculty of performing such operations; especially, when unqualified, the faculty of judging or deciding rightly, justly, or wisely.
ex: a man of judgment / a man of good judgment
a politician without judgment

senses.d: The conclusion or result of judging; an opinion; a decision.
ex: She in my judgment was as fair as you.

Not from the stars do I my judgment pluck;
And yet methinks I have astronomy […]

senses.d: The act of determining, as in courts of law, what is conformable to law and justice; also, the determination, decision, or sentence of a court, or of a judge.
ex: In judgments between the Rich and the Poor: it is not to be considered what the poor man needs, but what is his own
Most heartily I do beseech the court To give the judgment.

senses.d: The final award; the last sentence.

ety.text: Inherited from Old French jugement. By surface analysis, juger + -ment. Or from Late Latin iūdicāmentum, from Latin iūdicō (“to pass judgement upon”). Compare Occitan and Catalan jutjament; Old Italian giudicamento; Spanish juzgamiento; Portuguese julgamento.
Borrowed from Latin jūdicium, iūdicium.
Inherited from Old Spanish judizio, juyzio, borrowed from Latin iūdicium (“judgement, decision”) (compare Italian giudizio, Portuguese juízo).
Inherited from Late Latin jūdicāmentum, from Latin iūdex (“judge”). Equivalent to juzgar + -miento. Compare Portuguese julgamento, Catalan jutjament, French jugement, Italian giudicamento.
Probably a semi-learned term taken from Latin jūdicium, iūdicium. Compare Spanish juicio.

From Old Galician-Portuguese, from Late Latin iūdicāmentum, from Latin iūdex (“judge”). By surface analysis, julgar + -mento. Compare Spanish juzgamiento, Catalan and Occitan jutjament, French jugement, Italian giudicamento.
